title: Episode 254: Nikola Tesla: The Master of Lightning, the AC Induction Motor, and the Wireless Vision
description:
The enigmatic, visionary life of Nikola Tesla: the Serbian-born electrical wizard who conceived the rotating magnetic field, invented the polyphase alternating current induction motor, and harnessed the thundering cataracts of Niagara Falls to electrify a continent. Battling Thomas Edison in the War of the Currents, pioneering radio transmission, remote radio control, neon lighting, and producing artificial lightning bolts at his Colorado Springs laboratory, Tesla envisioned a wireless world system decades ahead of his time. Discover the poetic brilliance, eccentricity, and immortal genius of the man who created the twentieth century.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series explores the ethereal realm of high frequency, wireless energy, and artificial lightning: the life of the brilliant, tragic visionary who invented the alternating current system that powers planet earth. Here is George with the life of Nikola Tesla.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: BORN AT MIDNIGHT IN A LIGHTNING STORM: 1856 TO 1882
According to family legend, Nikola Tesla was born at the stroke of midnight during a terrifying summer electrical storm in July 1856 in the village of Smiljan, on the mountainous Croatian military frontier of the Austrian Empire. As lightning crashed over the house, the terrified midwife wrung her hands and declared the infant to be a child of darkness; his mother Georgina Mandic—an illiterate but gifted inventor of household tools—replied with fierce conviction: 'No, he will be a child of light.' From early childhood, Tesla possessed a mind of astonishing, photographic vitality, accompanied by intense, blinding flashes of light that appeared before his eyes whenever an idea formed. He could perform complex integral calculus entirely in his head, visualize machines in three dimensions down to the smallest bolt without drawing blueprints, and memorize entire books word for word. While studying engineering at the Joanneum Polytechnic School in Graz, Austria, Tesla watched a sputtering Gramme dynamo sparking violently on its direct current commutator, blurting out to his physics professor that direct current was an inefficient, mechanical dead end and that an alternating current motor could run without sparks or friction. The professor dismissed his idea as an impossible perpetual motion fantasy. In February 1882, while walking through the City Park in Budapest at sunset reciting Goethe's Faust, an electrifying revelation hit Tesla: drawing a diagram in the dirt with a walking stick, Tesla conceived the rotating magnetic field—the foundational principle of modern polyphase electrical machinery. Tesla's extraordinary photographic memory allowed him to visualize complex mechanical engines in operation, detecting micro-wear on imaginary gear teeth before a single metal casting was made. His epiphany in Budapest while quoting Goethe's Faust revealed the profound poetic nature of his scientific genius, reconciling classical literature with electromagnetic field theory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE JOURNEY TO AMERICA AND THE CLASH WITH EDISON: 1884 TO 1886
In June 1884, twenty-eight-year-old Nikola Tesla arrived in New York harbor with four cents in his pocket, a book of his own poetry, and a glowing letter of recommendation from Charles Batchelor, Edison's European manager, addressed to Thomas Alva Edison. The letter contained a legendary sentence: 'I know two great men and you are one of them; the other is this young man.' Edison hired Tesla immediately to repair direct current dynamos aboard the ocean liner SS Oregon. But the intellectual contrast between the two men was total: Edison was an unschooled, empirical pragmatist who solved problems through relentless trial and error; Tesla was a refined European theoretician steeped in classical poetry and mathematical precision. When Tesla proposed redesigning Edison's inefficient direct current dynamos to drastically boost performance, Edison allegedly promised him a bonus of fifty thousand dollars if he succeeded. Tesla labored eighteen hours a day for months, redesigning the dynamos and securing valuable patents for the company. When Tesla asked for his promised reward, Edison laughed coldly and dismissed the claim: 'Tesla, you don't understand our American humor.' Deeply disgusted by what he viewed as a dishonorable betrayal, Tesla resigned on the spot, walking into the bitter winter of 1886 to dig ditches in New York streets for two dollars a day to avoid starvation. Tesla's immigration to the United States was marked by tragedy and triumph: robbed of his steamship ticket and baggage in Paris, he arrived in Manhattan with nothing but his dreams and mathematical notebooks. The bitter ditch-digging winter of 1886 tested Tesla's spirit, yet he refused to surrender his belief in alternating current, using his evening hours to sketch improved polyphase motor designs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ALLIANCE WITH WESTINGHOUSE AND THE WAR OF THE CURRENTS
In 1887, impressed by Tesla's brilliance, a group of investors provided funding to establish the Tesla Electric Company on South Fifth Avenue. Within months, Tesla patented his masterwork: the polyphase alternating current induction motor and transformer system. In May 1888, Tesla delivered his historic lecture before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, demonstrating an electric motor that operated smoothly without brushes, commutators, or sparks by riding an invisible wave of rotating magnetic flux. In the audience sat Pittsburgh industrialist George Westinghouse, who instantly recognized that Tesla held the key to the electrical future. Westinghouse purchased Tesla's patents for sixty thousand dollars plus a generous royalty of two dollars and fifty cents per horsepower of electrical power generated. The alliance ignited the furious War of the Currents against Edison and J.P. Morgan's General Electric. In 1893, Westinghouse and Tesla triumphed decisively, winning the contract to illuminate the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago with a quarter-million alternating current lamps, turning the fairgrounds into a glowing 'White City' that dazzled twenty-seven million international visitors. When Westinghouse later faced bankruptcy due to Wall Street takeovers and begged Tesla for relief, Tesla tore up his multi-million-dollar royalty contract in a selfless gesture of friendship, forfeiting a personal fortune that would have made him the wealthiest man on earth. The demonstration before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers was an intellectual earthquake, proving that alternating current could drive heavy machinery without sparking commutators or friction. Tesla's selfless tearing up of his royalty contract saved George Westinghouse from financial ruin, cementing a lifelong fraternal friendship between the industrialist and the Serbian inventor.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: TAMING THE TORRENT: THE NIAGARA FALLS HYDROELECTRIC MIRACLE: 1895
Since childhood, Tesla had dreamed of harnessing the colossal mechanical energy of the thundering waterfalls he had read about in American schoolbooks. In 1893, an international commission headed by Lord Kelvin selected the Tesla polyphase alternating current system to harness the power of Niagara Falls. Constructing the Edward Dean Adams Power Plant, Westinghouse engineers installed three colossal five-thousand-horsepower Tesla two-phase generators driven by massive water turbines set in deep bedrock shafts beneath the roaring cataract. On the midnight of November 16, 1896, the master switch was thrown: instantly, fifteen thousand horsepower of clean, hydroelectric alternating current surged twenty-six miles down high-voltage transmission lines into the city of Buffalo, powering street railways and incandescent factories. Within years, Niagara electricity reached New York City four hundred miles away. The Niagara plant was an epochal milestone in human civilization: it proved that clean energy from rushing water could be transformed into high-voltage electricity and transmitted across immense continental distances to power human cities, validating Tesla's revolutionary electrical theories beyond all doubt. The engineering feat at Niagara Falls required excavating massive subterranean wheelpits through solid limestone, installing water turbines that rotated giant five-thousand-horsepower generators. When the power surged into Buffalo, electric streetcars began running on Niagara current, proving to the world that long-distance high-voltage transmission was the foundation of the modern electrified economy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: HIGH FREQUENCIES, THE TESLA COIL, AND THE COLORADO SPRINGS LIGHTNING: 1899
Moving beyond low-frequency power grids, Tesla became obsessed with the mysterious phenomena of high-frequency and high-voltage electricity, inventing the resonant transformer known as the Tesla Coil. In May 1899, Tesla moved his research to a remote wooden laboratory on the high plateau of Colorado Springs, constructing a colossal magnifying transmitter topped by an eighty-foot wooden tower and a three-foot copper sphere. Powering the transmitter with high-voltage currents, Tesla created artificial lightning bolts over one hundred and thirty-five feet in length, producing deafening thunderclaps heard twenty miles away in Cripple Creek and lighting two hundred wireless incandescent lamps planted directly in the dirt seven miles from the laboratory. Tesla claimed to have measured terrestrial stationary electrical waves, proving that the earth itself was a resonant conductor that could be vibrated electrically. In July 1899, while monitoring sensitive electrical receivers in the silence of the night, Tesla detected rhythmic, repetitive clicking signals that he believed were interplanetary communications from intelligent civilizations on Mars—igniting global headlines and capturing the Victorian imagination. The Colorado Springs laboratory was a site of cosmic wonder: the giant primary coil vibrated the ground for miles around, causing sparks to jump from horses' hooves and butterflies to glow with blue corona discharge. Tesla's belief that he had intercepted extraterrestrial signals from Mars reflected his profound conviction that human intelligence was not alone in the vast electromagnetic expanse of the universe.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TRAGIC DREAM OF WARDENCLYFFE: 1901 TO 1917
Returning to New York in 1900, Tesla envisioned a grand 'World Wireless System' that would combine global radio broadcasting, telegraphy, telephony, facsimile transmission, and wireless electrical power distribution into a single planetary network. Securing one hundred and fifty thousand dollars from financier J.P. Morgan, Tesla purchased two hundred acres at Shoreham on Long Island, commissioning legendary architect Stanford White to design the brick laboratory and a colossal one-hundred-and-eighty-seven-foot octagonal wooden tower capped by a fifty-five-ton steel hemispherical dome, anchored deep into the earth by a subterranean shaft. Known as Wardenclyffe, the facility was designed to beam wireless power and intelligence across the Atlantic Ocean. But in December 1901, Guglielmo Marconi used seventeen of Tesla's basic radio patents to transmit the Morse code letter 'S' across the Atlantic using a simple transmitter. Realizing that Tesla was pursuing wireless power rather than a commercial radio monopoly, Morgan withdrew his financial backing and refused further loans. Bankrupted, heartbroken, and unable to pay his debts, Tesla watched in despair as Wardenclyffe was abandoned, and in 1917 the magnificent tower was demolished for scrap metal. Wardenclyffe was intended as the crown jewel of human communication, capable of transmitting world news, music, private stock quotes, and marine navigation signals across oceans without a single wire. The demolition of the Wardenclyffe tower during World War I shattered Tesla's spirit, leaving the visionary inventor buried in crushing debts and forced to abandon his greatest scientific dream.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SOLITARY PROPHET OF NEW YORK AND THE IMMORTAL LEGACY
In his final decades, Nikola Tesla lived as an ascetic, reclusive philosopher in Suite 3327 of the Hotel New Yorker, feeding flocks of white pigeons in Bryant Park and nursing injured birds on his window ledge. While sensational newspapers labeled him an eccentric mad scientist chasing death rays and cosmic rays, Tesla continued to conceptualize revolutionary technologies: inventing the bladeless turbine, pioneering radio-guided robotic boats, and predicting modern smartphones, radar, and the Internet decades before their creation. In 1943, at age eighty-six, Tesla died peacefully in his sleep, penniless and alone in his hotel room. Months after his death, the United States Supreme Court overturned Marconi's radio patents, officially ruling that Nikola Tesla was the true original inventor of radio. Today, every alternating current motor, every high-voltage power line, every hydroelectric dam, and every wireless device on earth traces its lineage back to the fertile imagination of the Serbian boy born in a midnight thunderstorm. Nikola Tesla remains the ultimate patron saint of science: the man who illuminated a planet and dreamed of giving humanity the power of the stars. In his suite at the Hotel New Yorker, Tesla spent his evenings feeding pigeons in Bryant Park, claiming a mystical spiritual communion with a pure white dove that visited his window sill. The Supreme Court's posthumous recognition of Tesla's priority in radio technology restored his rightful place in history as the undisputed father of wireless telecommunications.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 255: Alexander Graham Bell—The Harmonic Telegraph, 'Mr. Watson, Come Here', and the World Connected. Until then, stay curious.
